Behoved
bē-hōvd´
v. (archaic: was necessary for, was fitting and required — rendering Greek dei)
Old English behofian, to have need of, to be needful. In the Authorized Version it carries the force of a divine necessity, not a mere propriety.

Biblical Definition

Behoved is the Authorized Version's word for what must be, and the New Testament uses it of the sufferings of Christ. On the Emmaus road and again in the upper room the risen Lord opens the Scriptures with it: “Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day” (Luk 24:46). The necessity is not physical but covenantal. Nothing compelled the Son of God from outside; the must arises from the eternal counsel of God and from the written word which that counsel had already given. Hence the Lord's earlier question in the same chapter: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?” (Luk 24:26). Hebrews applies the same word to the incarnation itself: “Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people” (Heb 2:17). The logic is exact. If He is to be a priest for men, He must be made like the men He represents; if He is to make reconciliation, He must have something to offer, and He must be able to die. The likeness was real and entire, sin excepted — He took part of the same flesh and blood (Heb 2:14), and by death destroyed him that had the power of death.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines behove as to be necessary for; to be fit or meet for; to be proper, or requisite in the circumstances of the case.

expand to see more

BEHOOVE, BEHOVE, v.t. To be necessary for; to be fit for; to be meet for, with respect to necessity, duty or convenience.

2. It is used chiefly impersonally: it behoveth, it behoved — that is, it is or was required by necessity or fitness.

3. In the Scriptures the word carries the force of a necessity arising from the purpose and promise of God, as, thus it behoved Christ to suffer.

BEHO'VED, pp. Was necessary or requisite for.

Key Scripture

Luke 24:46 — "And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day:"

Hebrews 2:17 — "Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people."

Luke 24:26 — "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?"

Hebrews 2:14 — "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;"

Modern Corruption

The necessity of the cross is denied outright, as though God might have forgiven without atonement, or reduced to tragic accident rather than eternal purpose.

expand to see more

The claim that God could simply have pardoned sin without the cross, and that the crucifixion was therefore an avoidable cruelty, runs directly against the Lord's own exposition. He did not say it was one way among several; He said it behoved Christ to suffer, and He said so out of the Scriptures. The necessity is grounded in God's own justice, which cannot clear the guilty without satisfaction, and in God's own promise, which had been written down beforehand. To call the atonement unnecessary is to make God's justice negotiable and His word provisional.

The opposite corruption empties the word of purpose and makes Calvary a miscarriage of Roman and Jewish justice that God afterward turned to good account. Peter's sermon closes that reading in a single sentence: Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and by wicked hands crucified and slain (Act 2:23). Both halves stand. The men who did it are guilty; the doing of it was decreed. Behoved is the word that holds the second half in place.

Hebrews 2:17 guards the incarnation against the same erosion. It behoved Him to be made like unto His brethren — not to appear so, not partially so, but really so, that He might be a merciful and faithful high priest. Every scheme that thins out the true humanity of Christ, ancient or modern, cuts the nerve of the priesthood, for a priest who is not of the people cannot represent them, and a body that cannot die cannot be offered.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dei (G1163), it is necessary, must needs — the impersonal verb of divine necessity, used of Christ's suffering, and opheilo (G3784), to owe, be bound, in Hebrews 2:17.

expand to see more

Greek dei (G1163) — it is necessary, it behoved; Luke 24:46, Luke 9:22, John 3:14, Acts 1:16.

Greek opheilo (G3784) — to owe, to be under obligation; Hebrews 2:17, where the necessity is that of the office He undertook.

Old English behofian, to have need of; the archaic English preserves an impersonal construction the modern tongue has lost.

The necessity is never external compulsion upon God, but the fitness required by His own justice and the certainty of His own promise.

Luke 24:26 puts the same necessity as a question — Ought not Christ to have suffered? — and expects the answer from the Scriptures.

Usage

"“Thus it behoved Christ to suffer” — opened out of the written word, not out of circumstance."

"“In all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren” — the priesthood requires the incarnation."

"The must of the cross is God's justice and God's promise, never man's compulsion."
